# Diverging bar graphs {#sec-diverging-bar-graphs} ::: {.callout-tip appearance='simple' icon=false} ***This graph is largely complete and just needs final proof reading.*** ::: :::: {.callout-note collapse="false" icon=false}
::: {.cell layout-align="right"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](diverging_bar_graphs_files/figure-html/full_code_display-1.png){fig-align='right' width=60% height=60%} ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #02577A;"} **Requirements:** ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.05em; color: #282b2d;"} **✅ a categorical variable** ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.05em; color: #282b2d;"} **✅ a numeric (continuous) variable** ::: :::: ## Description If you have two proportions that contain positive and negative values, consider using diverging bars with `geom_bar()`. Unlike a standard or stacked bar graphs, diverging bar graphs display positive and negative quantities on both sides of a reference or baseline value (zero in this example). Color, length and position are used to compare the quantities across categorical levels (and within variable values). ### Horizontal bars ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](diverging_bar_graphs_files/figure-html/diverg-1.png){fig-align='center' width=75% height=75%} ::: ::: For example, we can use the length of the bar from the reference line to compare Britannica's share across all years (i.e., comparing the brown bars to each other). ### Vertical bars ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](diverging_bar_graphs_files/figure-html/diverg_vert-1.png){fig-align='center' width=75% height=75%} ::: ::: We can also compare Encarta vs. Britannica within each year (i.e., compare the blue vs. brown bars to each other within each year). ## Set up ::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"} **PACKAGES:** ::: Install packages. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} library(ggplot2) library(dplyr) # for data manipulation library(tidyr) # for uncount() ``` ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"} **DATA:** ::: In the 90s, the family encyclopedia moved from a shelf of hardcover volumes to a single CD-ROM. Microsoft's *Encarta* (1993) was cheap and came bundled with new PCs, and the *Encyclopedia Britannica* lost ground every year. We'll simulate a yearly survey of 400 households from 1993 to 1999 asking which encyclopedia they used most: Encarta, Britannica, or something else (`Other`). Encarta's chance of being picked grows each year (`p_encarta`), Britannica gets what's left of 80% (`p_britannica`), and `Other` stays at 20%. For each household, `runif()` draws a number between 0 and 1, and `case_when()` turns that number into a choice using the year's probabilities. Then we keep Encarta and Britannica, calculate each one's share of the 400 households, and make Britannica's share negative so it points down. Setting the seed with `set.seed()` means you'll get the same 2,800 households every time you run the code below. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} set.seed(1993) encyclopedia_survey <- tibble(year = 1993:1999) |> mutate(p_encarta = 0.8 * plogis(-2 + 0.6 * (year - 1993)), p_britannica = 0.8 - p_encarta) |> tidyr::uncount(400, .id = "household") |> mutate(u = runif(n()), choice = case_when(u < p_encarta ~ "Encarta", u < p_encarta + p_britannica ~ "Britannica", TRUE ~ "Other")) |> select(year, household, choice) encarta_diverg <- encyclopedia_survey |> filter(choice != "Other") |> count(year, choice) |> mutate(share = n / 400, share = if_else(choice == "Britannica", -share, share), choice = factor(choice, levels = c("Encarta", "Britannica")), year = factor(year)) glimpse(encarta_diverg) #> Rows: 14 #> Columns: 4 #> $ year 1993, 1993, 1994, 1994, 1995, 199… #> $ choice Britannica, Encarta, Britannica, … #> $ n 275, 30, 244, 65, 219, 94, 181, 1… #> $ share -0.6875, 0.0750, -0.6100, 0.1625,… ``` ::: ::: ## Distribution A diverging bar graph puts two shares back to back, so the question it answers is "how do these two groups trade places?" Here, every household picks exactly one encyclopedia each year, so a gain for Encarta has to come from somewhere. Below we'll move from the households, to a picture, to the formula. ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **COUNT IT:** ::: Start with the first ten households surveyed in 1993. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} head(encyclopedia_survey$choice, 10) #> [1] "Britannica" "Encarta" "Britannica" #> [4] "Britannica" "Britannica" "Britannica" #> [7] "Britannica" "Britannica" "Other" #> [10] "Encarta" ``` ::: ::: Seven of these ten households used Britannica, two used Encarta, and one used something else. Counting every household in every year shows the trade: Britannica's count falls each year while Encarta's climbs, and `Other` stays between about 60 and 100. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} encyclopedia_survey |> count(year, choice) |> tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = choice, values_from = n) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **DRAW IT:** ::: A bar model shows each year's 400 households as one bar split three ways. Reading down the years, the Encarta part grows, the Britannica part shrinks, and the `Other` part barely moves. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} encyclopedia_survey |> count(year, choice) |> mutate(choice = factor(choice, levels = c("Encarta", "Britannica", "Other"))) |> ggplot(aes(x = n, y = factor(year), fill = choice)) + geom_col(position = position_stack(reverse = TRUE)) + labs(x = "Households", y = "Year", fill = "Encyclopedia") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](diverging_bar_graphs_files/figure-html/draw_bar_model_diverging_bar-1.png){width=576} ::: ::: ::: The diverging bar graph below takes the Encarta and Britannica parts of each bar and points them in opposite directions from zero. The points mark the shares we built into the simulation. The two bars are the same length somewhere between 1996 and 1997, which is where the two encyclopedias traded places. ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} expected_shares <- tibble(year = 1993:1999) |> mutate(Encarta = 0.8 * plogis(-2 + 0.6 * (year - 1993)), Britannica = -(0.8 - Encarta), year = factor(year)) |> tidyr::pivot_longer(-year, names_to = "choice", values_to = "share") ggplot(data = encarta_diverg, aes(x = year, y = share)) + geom_bar(aes(fill = choice), stat = "identity", width = .5) + geom_point(data = expected_shares, size = 2.5) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0) + scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-1, 1), labels = scales::percent) + labs(x = "Year", y = "Share of households", fill = "Encyclopedia") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](diverging_bar_graphs_files/figure-html/draw_diverging_bar-1.png){width=576} ::: ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.10em; color: #1e83c8;"} **NAME IT:** ::: Each household's answer is a single draw from three choices, so each year's counts follow a [multinomial distribution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multinomial_distribution): $$ (N_{\text{Encarta}}, N_{\text{Britannica}}, N_{\text{Other}}) \sim \text{Multinomial}\left(400, \; (p_t, \; 0.8 - p_t, \; 0.2)\right) $$ $$ p_t = 0.8 \times \text{logistic}\left(-2 + 0.6\,(t - 1993)\right) $$ The logistic function (`plogis()`) gives Encarta's share an S shaped climb: slow at first, fastest in the middle, then leveling off. Encarta and Britannica split the same 80%, so their bars are the same length when $p_t = 0.4$. That happens when $-2 + 0.6\,(t - 1993) = 0$, or $t \approx 1996.3$. Each simulated share wobbles around its point by about $\sqrt{p(1 - p) / 400}$, which is never more than 2.5 percentage points. That's why the bars land so close to the points. Try changing the `0.6` in `plogis()` and the crossover moves earlier (larger values) or later (smaller values). ## Grammar ::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"} **CODE:** ::: - Create labels with `labs()` - Initialize the graph with `ggplot()` and provide `data` - Map the `year` to the `x` and `share` to the `y` - Inside` geom_bar()` - map `choice` to `fill` - use `stat = "identity"` and `width = .5` - Add `scale_y_continuous()` to manually set the limits and format the axis with `scales::percent` ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="show"} labs_geom_bar_diverg <- labs( title = "Encarta vs. Britannica (simulated)", subtitle = "Encyclopedia households used most each year", x = "Year", y = "Share of households", fill = "Encyclopedia") ggp2_bars_diverg <- ggplot( data = encarta_diverg, aes(x = year, y = share)) + geom_bar(aes(fill = choice), stat = "identity", width = .5) + scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-1, 1), labels = scales::percent) ggp2_bars_diverg + labs_geom_bar_diverg ``` ::: ::: ::: {style="font-size: 1.15em; color: #1e83c8;"} **GRAPH:** ::: ::: {.cell layout-nrow="1"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](diverging_bar_graphs_files/figure-html/create_graph_diverging_bar-1.png){width=100% height=100%} ::: ::: ## More info For vertically arranged bars, we switch the `x` and `y` axis variables. ### Vertically arranged bars
- Create labels with `labs()` - Map the `share` to the `x` and `year` to the `y` - *Inside* `geom_bar()` - map `choice` to `fill` - use `stat = "identity"` and `width = .5` - Add `scale_x_continuous()` to manually set the limits and format the axis with `scales::percent` ::: {style="font-size: 0.85em;"} ::: {.cell layout-nrow="1"} ```{.r .cell-code} labs_geom_bar_diverg_vert <- labs( title = "Encarta vs. Britannica (simulated)", subtitle = "Encyclopedia households used most each year", x = "Share of households", y = "Year", fill = "Encyclopedia") ggp2_bar_diverg_vert <- ggplot( data = encarta_diverg, aes(x = share, y = year)) + geom_bar( aes(fill = choice), stat = "identity", width = .5) + scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-1, 1), labels = scales::percent) ggp2_bar_diverg_vert + labs_geom_bar_diverg_vert ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](diverging_bar_graphs_files/figure-html/create_graph_vert_diverg_bars-1.png){width=100% height=100%} ::: ::: :::
